title: Reservoir-prefetch continuous scheduler for mixed prompt/response workloads
creator: Aisha Qureshi
description:
Problem: Our existing continuous-batcher treats incoming requests homogeneously, which leads to inefficient KV residency and GPU slab fragmentation for workloads with a heavy mix of short prompts and long responses (conversations with very asymmetric token distributions). This results in higher tail latency for long responses and increased peak GPU memory usage under bursty traffic.

Goal: Implement a reservoir-prefetch scheduling layer that groups incoming requests into micro-reservoirs by turn-length profile and prefix residence score, prefetches KV shards proactively for high-residency cohorts, and triggers gentle KV compaction for low-residency cohorts to free slab space. The controller should be adaptive (learns per-customer length distributions) and prioritize latency-sensitive traffic while preserving throughput.

Proposed approach:
- Introduce a lightweight "reservoir" classification computed at ingress: short-prompt, long-response-heavy, interleaved-dialogue. Classification uses sequence-length histogram + recent turn autocorrelation.
- Allocate micro-reservoir slots on each GPU worker: N_short, N_long, N_mixed. Slots are soft-guarantees; unused capacity floats.
- Prefetch policy: when a request is admitted into a reservoir, compute a prefetch score combining KV coldness, recently seen prefix reuse, and predicted continuation length. If above threshold, prefetch KV into a reserved hot slab region.
- KV slab management: implement a two-tier slab allocator (hot/reservoir vs. cold/evictable) with an async compaction worker that compacts cold slab pages during low utilization windows.
- Eviction: use residency heatmaps per-token-position to evict entries with low future-use probability; avoid evicting prefixes actively used by short-turn cohorts.
- Admission & pacing: use reservoir backpressure to slow admission from long-response cohorts when hot slab pressure is high; allow short prompts to bypass (low latency) with limited reservation.
- Telemetry & rollout: add reservoir-specific metrics (reservoir_hit_rate, slab_fill_hot, prefetched_kv_bytes, prefetch_miss_penalty_ms) and dashboards. Canary rollout with 5% traffic, compare p99 latency for long-response class and GPU memory headroom.

Trade-offs & constraints:
- Prefetch saves p99 for long responses but increases memory pressure; mitigated by hot/cold slab split and async compaction.
- Classification adds CPU overhead at ingress (~0.15ms per request in a microbenchmark). Acceptable but must be tuned.
- Risk of increased fragmentation from hot-region churn — mitigated via compaction policy and larger slab buckets for long-response cohorts.

Success criteria:
- p99 latency for long-response class reduced by >= 10% in controlled load tests.
- Peak GPU memory down by >= 6% after compaction vs baseline when using identical traffic.
- No more than 2% overall throughput regression in steady-state.

Artifacts & links:
- Design doc: https://confluence.internal.redwood.ai/display/SRV/Reservoir+Prefetch+Scheduler
- Prototype PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving/pull/4128
- Benchmark dashboard (perflab): https://dash.internal.redwood.ai/d/perf/reservoir-prefetch-2026q1

Rollout plan:
1) Unit tests + microbenchmarking (local perf lab).
2) Deploy prototype behind feature flag in staging; run replay with mixlen traces.
3) Canary on 5% production traffic (runtime-1.21), monitor reservoir metrics and memory headroom.
4) Gradual ramp with automated rollback on memory pressure or tail-latency increase.

Notes: This ticket focuses on scheduler and KV residency policy; actual kernel/quantization tuning will be done in follow-up tickets once the allocation pattern stabilizes.
